summary: Describes IAX, the Inter-Asterisk eXchange protocol, an application-layer protocol for creating, modifying, and ending multimedia sessions, mostly VoIP calls. It was created by the open source community for the Asterisk PBX and handles both call control and media in one protocol. This is an informational document, later updated by RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: IAX Version 2 carries call setup and media over the same UDP association. It uses reliable frames for control and smaller, unreliable frames for time-sensitive media.

questions: what is the difference between iax and sip
subtitle: A protocol that carries call control and multimedia over one UDP association.

tldr.problem: Multimedia systems often use separate protocols and network paths for call control and media, creating extra overhead and NAT traversal challenges.
tldr.mechanism: IAX combines control and media in binary frames over UDP port 4569. Reliable Full Frames carry control; Mini Frames carry media without retransmission.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5456 is an Informational independent submission and has been updated by RFC 8996. It is not an Internet Standards Track specification.

today: RFC 5456 is an Informational document published at the RFC Editor's discretion, not an Internet Standard. It has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: What IAX Combines
sections.content:
Inter-Asterisk eXchange (IAX) is an application-layer protocol for creating, changing, and ending multimedia sessions over IP. The RFC describes Version 2, developed by the open source community for the Asterisk private branch exchange and aimed mainly at voice calls.

IAX carries signaling and media over one UDP stream between peers, using the same well-known port, 4569. The RFC describes this unified path as simplifying NAT traversal and firewall management. IAX is binary and optimized for low-overhead voice traffic, though the RFC also identifies limits such as its fixed-size codec mask and the risks of a well-known port.
sections.plainLanguage: IAX carries both call instructions and the voice stream between peers using one UDP association. This keeps the protocol's path simple, while its design also has limitations described in the RFC.

sections.title: Registering a Peer
sections.content:
Registration is optional. A registrant tells a registrar the network address where a resource can be reached, along with credentials if requested. The registrant sends REGREQ; the registrar may request authentication with REGAUTH, then accept with REGACK or reject with REGREJ.

The RFC describes MD5 challenge-response and RSA public-key authentication. A registration has a refresh period. If no period is supplied, the peers use a default expiry of 60 seconds; a registration not renewed in time must be invalidated.
sections.plainLanguage: A peer can register the address where it can be reached. It must renew the registration before it expires, and the registrar can ask it to prove its identity.

sections.title: Setting Up and Ending Calls
sections.content:
An IAX call can consist of one or more call legs. Each leg has identifiers chosen by both peers. A caller begins with a NEW message; the receiving peer responds with a rejection, authentication request, acceptance, or hangup. After acceptance, messages indicate progress, ringing, busy status, or answer.

The RFC also describes call-path optimization. If adjacent call legs use IAX and an intermediate peer no longer needs to remain in the path, peers can confirm a new path. They do not change the path until all peers in that path confirm they can communicate.
sections.plainLanguage: A call leg starts with a request and an answer from the other peer. If a middle peer can leave the path, IAX waits until every peer in the new path confirms it works.

sections.title: Full, Mini, and Meta Frames
sections.content:
A frame is IAX's basic communication unit. Full Frames carry control and signaling and include call identifiers, sequencing information, a timestamp, and a frame type. They are reliable and require acknowledgment. Their header is 12 octets.

Mini Frames carry media for an established call. They use a 4-octet header and are sent unreliably because retransmitted voice data may arrive too late to use. Their timestamp is the low 16 bits of the call timestamp and wraps; a Full Frame should be sent to signal resynchronization. Meta Frames support video or combine multiple media streams in a trunk.
sections.plainLanguage: Full Frames carry control messages that need reliable delivery. Mini Frames carry time-sensitive media with a shorter header, and Meta Frames carry video or group media streams together.

sections.title: Security and Operational Limits
sections.content:
The RFC describes registration and call authentication using MD5 or RSA and a framework for native encryption. It notes that call details remain unencrypted even when a call's media is encrypted. Without encryption, audio and video can be intercepted, and messages may be altered by an attacker on the path.

The RFC also discusses denial-of-service risks from IAX's single well-known port and from resource exhaustion. It notes that distinct registration errors may reveal whether a username exists. These are concerns and mechanisms described by the memo, not a guarantee that every deployment uses them.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication and encryption can protect parts of an IAX call, but the RFC notes that call details may still be visible. It also describes risks from attacks on the shared port and registration process.
